draft.title: Organising ideas in paragraphs
card: A paragraph develops one main idea. It usually opens with a topic sentence that states that idea.
The sentences after it support the idea with evidence, examples or explanation. They stay on the topic sentence's idea.
When the writer moves to a new idea, they start a new paragraph. Linking words such as however, also or as a result show how paragraphs connect.
The order of paragraphs matters. In an argument, each paragraph builds on the last towards the writer's point. In a story, the order builds events towards the ending.
draft.remember: One idea for each paragraph, opened by a topic sentence, and ordered to build towards the point.

a.q: What is the main job of a topic sentence?
opts: To state the one idea the paragraph will develop
To give the strongest piece of evidence in the paragraph
To finish the paragraph by repeating the writer's point
To link the paragraph to the title of the text
a.why: A topic sentence names the idea the rest of the paragraph supports. Evidence comes in the sentences after it, so giving the strongest evidence is the job of those sentences, not the topic sentence.

b.q: Jess is writing about why her town needs a skate park. Her paragraph opens with a topic sentence about a safe place for teenagers to meet. Which sentence belongs in this paragraph?
opts: Supervised spaces mean fewer teenagers gather in car parks
The council should also repair the town's footpaths
Skate parks were first built in the United States
Local shops would earn more from extra visitors
b.why: The topic sentence is about a safe place for teenagers, and the correct option supports that idea. The shop sentence supports a different idea, the benefit to business, so it needs its own paragraph.
b.clue: Stay on the idea of safety.

a.best: To state the one idea the paragraph will develop

b.best: Supervised spaces mean fewer teenagers gather in car parks
